payload.title: Crypto ATM Numbers Fall to 2021 Levels Amid Regulatory Crackdown – Bitcoin News
payload.description: Global crypto ATM numbers fall to 2021 levels as U.S. state bans accelerate removals, leaving just 27,358 machines worldwide.
payload.content: The number of global crypto ATMs has fallen to 27,358 as of late September 2026, reaching levels last seen in 2021, with 587 machines removed since July 8, 2026. payload.title: Bitcoin hashrate falls to 3-week low as miners cut BTC
payload.description: Bitcoin’s seven-day hashrate fell to a three-week low as miner reserves dropped 1,530 BTC and the Puell Multiple rose to 1.13.
payload.content:
Bitcoin’s seven-day average network hashrate dropped to 915.8 EH/s between Sept. 20–26, its lowest in three weeks. This decline, down about 34.86 million TH/s week-over-week, reflects reduced computing power securing the network; daily readings frequently fell below one zettahash, after surpassing that threshold earlier in September. CoinWarz reported hashrate near 954 EH/s on Sept. 25, down from 984 EH/s on Sept. 24, and cited significant volatility during the month, including peaks above 1 ZH/s on Sept. 9 and 15. According to Twenty One Capital CEO Raphael Zagury, this marks Bitcoin’s first “hashrate bear market,” with network strength falling roughly 22%–24% from late-2025 peaks, partly as mining firms shift capacity toward AI computing.

Miner Bitcoin reserves decreased by 1,530 BTC over the week, reaching approximately 1,192,766 BTC. These outflows, reported by CryptoQuant and Digital Asset, do not necessarily signify exchange sales; reserves can drop due to sales, transfers, lending, or other treasury activities. In early September, miner reserves had briefly increased by 261 BTC. Policies vary: CleanSpark mined 593 BTC but sold 821 BTC in August, ending the month with 13,703 BTC and an operating hashrate of 38.3 EH/s. Hyperscale Data ceased mining at its Michigan site on Sept. 1 for an AI contract, reducing holdings by 79% (from 1,006 BTC in July to around 215 BTC).

The Puell Multiple, measuring daily miner revenue to the one-year average, rose by 0.24 to 1.13 on Sept. 26. Other dashboards showed neutral readings (~1.01), estimating daily miner issuance at 450 BTC and revenue at $37.8 million. Bitcoin’s current block subsidy remains 3.125 BTC after April 2024 halving; the next reduction to 1.5625 BTC is projected for 2028.

Regional mining conditions are uneven. Ethiopia cut electricity supplied to miners to 23% of contracted levels amid reduced reservoir inflows, after mining used nearly one-third of national electricity and generated 35% of utility revenue last year. The utility will review conditions in October. Despite the hashrate dip, block production continued normally, as the difficulty adjustment mechanism responds every 2,016 blocks.

payload.title: Bitget hacker routes 4 BTC through Wasabi CoinJoin

Circle has the capacity to freeze USDC at specified addresses, but it is unclear if a legal order has reached them.
Bitget states the vulnerability responsible for the breach is fixed and will reopen withdrawals in phases: Bitcoin at 08:00 UTC on Sept. 28; ETH on Sept. 29; USDT on Sept. 30; other tokens, fiat, and peer-to-peer withdrawals on Oct. 2. Mandiant and SlowMist assist with the ongoing investigation. Bitget’s Protection Fund (over $464 million) will cover losses; user balances remain unchanged. payload.description: TL;DRCircle is taking another piece of traditional financial infrastructure onchain, this time targeting the foreign exchange market.StableFX is now live on Arc, Circle’s blockchain network, with the service designed to let approved institutions exchange stablecoin-denominated currencies around the…
payload.content:
Circle has launched StableFX on Arc, its blockchain network, enabling approved institutions to settle foreign exchange (FX) trades with stablecoin-denominated currencies 24/7, surpassing conventional banking and settlement windows. StableFX uses request-for-quote (RFQ) pricing from multiple liquidity providers and smart-contract-based settlement, where both sides of a trade fund a settlement contract, ensuring payment-versus-payment (PvP) settlement: both legs of the trade settle simultaneously, or neither does. This structure reduces principal risk, the scenario where one party sends currency before receiving the other. Institutions can opt for immediate settlement or programmable windows, allowing trades to be netted before final settlement, reflecting traditional backend financial infrastructure more than crypto-native payment systems.

The service supports multiple stablecoins, including Circle’s USDC and EURC, as well as tokens representing Australian dollar, Brazilian real, Japanese yen, Canadian dollar, and South African rand. Circle Technology Services provides the API and smart contract infrastructure but does not act as a custodian or intermediary holding customer funds, leaving licensing and compliance responsibilities to participating firms.

Circle aims to eliminate settlement friction in the global FX market by bringing this infrastructure onchain, leveraging stablecoins’ proven ability to move money quickly and safely. StableFX is testing whether regulated institutions can use these rails to efficiently exchange currencies, manage settlement risk, and keep capital productive outside traditional market hours. If widely adopted, the most significant stablecoin use case could be institutional backend settlements rather than consumer crypto payments. The Act is set to take full effect by January 18, 2027, or 120 days after final regulations are published, with a three-year grace period ending July 18, 2028, for full compliance.

Key provisions include:
- Stablecoins must be backed 1:1 by high-quality liquid assets (e.g., U.S. Treasuries, central bank reserves).
- Payment stablecoins are reclassified as neither securities nor commodities but as unique instruments under banking regulators (OCC, Federal Reserve).
- Issuers must maintain 100% reserves and provide holders with legal priority in insolvency, similar to bank deposits.
- Strict AML/KYC requirements and technical ability to "freeze and burn" assets upon law enforcement request.
- A "rebuttable presumption" (the "Yield Ban") prohibits issuers and affiliates from paying interest or rewards on stablecoins; indirect rewards are also scrutinized.
- Issuers with over $10 billion in circulation must transition to federal supervision; smaller issuers remain under state-certified regimes.
- Minimum capital floor for issuers is $5 million.

Timeline milestones:
- July 18, 2025: Act enacted.
- February 25, 2026: OCC releases 376-page NPRM detailing capital requirements and licensing.
- May 2026: 60-day comment period for industry feedback ends.
- January 18, 2027: Statutory effective date; new issuances must comply.
- July 18, 2028: All secondary market trading must be in compliant tokens.

The Act brings legitimacy and user protection but centralizes the market, raises compliance costs, and restricts yield opportunities. U.S. exchanges must delist non-compliant stablecoins by 2027. The Act applies only to payment stablecoins, not all cryptocurrencies.
